result.topic_en: Euler works out the special case m=4 (order n+4) of his relation between the coefficients p and q, then begins §29, treating the cases n=1 and n=2 for general m.
result.transcription:
172 MEDITATIONES CIRCA
IV. Sit $m=4$, ordinisque exponens $n+4$, et
$q^{\mu}+q^{n+4-\mu}=p^{\mu}+p^{n+4}$, et aequatio noſtra fiet
$0=q^4-n(q^3+q^{n+1})+\frac{n(n+1)}{1.\,2}(q^2+q^{n+2})-\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{1.\,2.\,3}(q+q^{n+3})$
$+\frac{n(nn+5)}{1.\,2.\,3}p^{n+4}$
$+q^n+4q^{n-1}+10q^{n-2}+20q^{n-3}\dots\dots+\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{1.\,2.\,3}q$
$-\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)}{1.\,2.\,3.\,4}p^{n+4}$
ſiue
$q^n+4q^{n-1}+10q^{n-2}\dots+\frac{(n+1)n(n-1)}{1.\,2.\,3}q^2=\frac{n(n-1)(nn+3n+14)}{24}p^{n+4}$
$+q^4-n(q^3+q^{n+1})+\frac{n(n+1)}{1.\,2}(q^2+q^{n+2})-\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{1.\,2.\,3}q^{n+3}$.
29. Euoluamus etiam ſimili modo quosdam caſus pro exponente $n$.
I. Sit primo $n=1$, et ordinis exponens $m+1$, eritque noſtra aequatio
$0=q^m-q^{m-1}+q^{m-2}-q^{m-3}\dots\mp q\pm\frac{1}{2}$[?]$]p^{m+1}\pm q\mp p^{m+1}$
$-q^2+q^3-q^4\dots\mp q^m$
vnde patet ſi $m$ fuerit numerus par, quo caſu ſuperiora ſigna valent, totam aequationem fieri identicam; at ſi $m$ ſit numerus impar habebitur
$q^2-q^3+q^4-q^5\dots-q^m=\frac{1}{2}p^{m+1}$.
II. Sit $n=2$, ordinisque exponens $m+2$, et aequatio noſtra erit
$0=q^m-2q^{m-1}+3q^{m-2}-4q^{m-3}\dots\mp mq\;+\frac{1}{2}(m+2)\Big\}p^{m+2}$
$-2q^3+3q^4-4q^5\dots\mp mq^{m+1}-\frac{1}{2}(m+1)\Big\}$
$\pm q^2\pm mq\mp(m+1)p^{m+2}$
vbi ſuperior ambiguitas valet pro valoribus paribus ipſius $m$, inferior pro imparibus. Iam pro variis valoribus ipſius $m$ habebimus.
Primo

items.quote:
vnde patet ſi $m$ fuerit numerus par, quo caſu ſuperiora ſigna valent, totam aequationem fieri identicam; at ſi $m$ ſit numerus impar habebitur
$q^2-q^3+q^4-q^5\dots-q^m=\frac{1}{2}p^{m+1}$.
items.english: Whence it is clear that if m is an even number, in which case the upper signs apply, the whole equation becomes an identity; but if m is an odd number, we shall have q^2 - q^3 + q^4 - q^5 ... - q^m = (1/2) p^{m+1}.

items.quote: Euoluamus etiam ſimili modo quosdam caſus pro exponente $n$.
items.english: Let us also work out, in a similar way, some cases for the exponent n.
